Saxony
SAK-so-nee
n. (the electorate of Wittenberg, where the Reformation began, and whose division between two Saxon houses nearly destroyed it)
Latin Saxonia, from the Saxons; German Sachsen. The lands were divided in 1485 between the Ernestine and Albertine lines of the house of Wettin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Saxony is where the Reformation began and where it was first betrayed from inside. Wittenberg, in Ernestine or electoral Saxony, held the university at which Luther taught from 1512 and the church door on which the ninety-five theses were posted in 1517; Frederick the Wise protected him, John the Steadfast presented the Augsburg Confession in 1530, and John Frederick led the Schmalkaldic League. Ducal or Albertine Saxony, under Duke George, stayed Catholic until 1539. Then in 1546 Duke Maurice of Albertine Saxony took the emperor's side against his own cousin and co-religionist for the promise of the electoral title; the League was broken at Muhlberg in 1547, John Frederick was imprisoned, and Maurice received the electorate. It was Maurice's Saxony that then accepted the Leipzig Interim of 1548, conceding the restoration of Catholic ceremonies, bishops and much of the mass on the ground that these were things indifferent, adiaphora, which a church might yield to keep the peace. Matthias Flacius and the strict Lutherans refused, the quarrel split the Lutheran churches for thirty years, and the Formula of Concord settled it in 1577 against the Interim. The dictionary enters Saxony because the Reformation's birthplace produced its sharpest lesson: that a concession called indifferent is not indifferent when it is demanded as the price of surrender.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an interim as the meantime or intervening time; adiaphora as things indifferent; an elector as a prince entitled to vote for the emperor; and a concession as the act of yielding.

expand to see more

INTERIM, n. The meantime; the intervening time; a temporary arrangement made until a final settlement.

INDIFFERENT, a. Neither good nor bad; having no influence or preponderating weight; of a middle nature.

ELECTOR, n. A prince of the German empire who had a voice in the election of the emperor.

CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded, usually implying a demand or claim.

CEREMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion; the forms of civility; outward form.

Key Scripture

Gal 2:5 — "To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you."

Gal 5:1 — "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage."

Col 2:16 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:"

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Electorate of Wittenberg where the Reformation began, divided between Ernestine and Albertine houses, whose Leipzig Interim of 1548 conceded ceremonies as things indifferent.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the yielding of a thing truly indifferent at the moment when yielding it is a confession of defeat. The Leipzig Interim's defenders were not wrong that vestments and feast days are not commanded or forbidden in themselves; they were wrong that a ceremony demanded by a victorious enemy as the sign of submission is still merely a ceremony. The apostle makes the distinction himself: he circumcised Timothy freely and refused Titus absolutely, and of the latter case he says “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour” (Gal 2:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that liberty is to be stood in and not traded. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1) is the command Flacius acted on, and the dictionary judges that he was right and Melanchthon's party wrong, while recording that their motive was the preservation of the churches and not cowardice. The rule for things genuinely indifferent remains, that no man is to judge another “in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday” (Col 2:16), and the rule for the rest is to “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; Greek hupotage (G5292), subjection; Greek hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, an outline.

expand to see more

Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection, a yielding under; “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour”, Galatians 2:5.

Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free”, Galatians 5:1.

Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke, a burden borne; “be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage”, Galatians 5:1.

Greek heorte (G1859) — a feast, a holy day; “in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday”, Colossians 2:16.

Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern to be kept; “Hold fast the form of sound words”, 2 Timothy 1:13.

Usage

"“To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour” (Gal 2:5) — the Leipzig Interim of 1548 and Flacius's refusal."

"“Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1) — Maurice's bargain and Muhlberg, 1547."

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — thirty years of quarrel ended by the Formula of Concord."
